sections.content: You know *con tal de que* and *a menos que* from B1 Unit 21, *salvo que* from B2 Unit 9 and *siempre y cuando* from B2 Unit 11: conditions that take the subjunctive. Rules and contracts use them to say exactly when something applies. Here is one more, *en caso de que* "in the event that". It names a case that may happen and says what follows: *En caso de que un socio no pueda abonar la cuota, deberá avisar a la junta*. A rule usually puts the condition first and the consequence in the future with *deberá* or *podrá*, so the reader sees at once when it applies.

sections.title: Four conditions
rows: En caso de que el socio no pueda cultivar su parcela, deberá avisar a la junta.
If the member cannot cultivate his plot, he must notify the board. (a case that may happen)
La parcela podrá cederse siempre y cuando la junta lo apruebe.
The plot may be transferred as long as the board approves. (a strict condition)
El contrato se prorrogará salvo que alguna de las partes avise con antelación.
The contract is renewed unless one of the parties gives notice in advance. (the only exception)
El socio podrá ceder la parcela, con tal de que lo notifique por escrito.
The member may transfer the plot, provided he gives notice in writing. (a requirement)

items.spanish: En caso de que haya dudas, la junta decidirá.
items.english: In the event of doubt, the board will decide.

items.spanish: La baja será efectiva previo aviso por escrito.
items.english: The withdrawal takes effect after notice in writing.

items.spanish: Los socios podrán pedir una prórroga siempre y cuando lo notifiquen a tiempo.
items.english: Members may ask for an extension as long as they give notice in time.

items.spanish: El plazo no vencerá salvo que la junta lo decida.
items.english: The deadline will not expire unless the board decides so.

sections.content: English "in case" is a precaution ("take a coat in case it rains"). In a rule, *En caso de que* names a condition ("if it happens that"), not a precaution. Always write *en caso de que*, with *de*; *en caso que* is a common slip (compare *de que* and *que* in C1 Unit 2). And keep the subjunctive after all four phrases: the case has not happened yet.
